item.title: Continued fractions and passive ladder networks for acoustic impedances: the baffled piston and the horn
item.description: arXiv:2610.20371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lumped-element networks give transparent, passive models of acoustic impedances whose low- and high-frequency limits can be read from the circuit, but a systematic, arbitrarily accurate construction for non-rational impedances is lacking. Continued fractions, one- and two-point Pad\'e approximants and their identity with ladder networks and Cauer synthesis are introduced in tutorial form and applied to two examples: the radiation impedance of a baffled circular piston and the throat impedance of a horn with a piston mouth. The even contraction of the piston's continued fraction has positive coefficients, certified by interval arithmetic for the first 100 pairs, and yields a ladder of positive resistances, masses and compliances; with 14 elements the error is 4e-4 up to ka = 5. Beranek's four-element network is, to about 2%, the order-two two-point Pad\'e approximant. A horn modelled as a cascade of waveguide sections is a continued fraction whose tail is the mouth impedance; the infinite exponential horn is a periodic continued fraction, an exact high-pass ladder. The piston networks are passive at every certified order (up to 202 elements) and are extended without changing existing elements; for a finite horn the error of the mouth network passes one to one to the throat impedance.
item.dc:creator: Ronald M. Aarts

item.title: The Soul of Waves: Physical Interpretation of Dispersion Relations
item.description: arXiv:2601.17098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This pedagogical paper presents a comprehensive framework for interpreting dispersion relations across fundamental physical systems. We adopt a novel approach that starts from the mathematical form $\omega(\mathbf{k})$ and systematically extracts its physical content, rather than deriving it from first principles. Through an in-depth case study of the massive Klein-Gordon dispersion relation $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + c^2k^2$, we demonstrate how this single equation encodes phase velocity, group velocity, density of states, effective mass, and impedance. The analysis reveals the universal nature of this dispersion form, which manifests in quantum fields, plasmas, superconductors, and photonic crystals with different physical interpretations of its parameters. We complement this with detailed examination of classical systems including mass-spring chains and hydrodynamic waves, providing tangible analogies that bridge conceptual understanding between quantum and classical wave phenomena. The paper includes eleven carefully designed figures that visualize key concepts and a comprehensive catalog of dispersion relations in the Appendix. Aimed at advanced undergraduates and instructors, this work emphasizes conceptual understanding through physical interpretation, offering a unified pedagogical framework for teaching wave propagation across physics curricula while maintaining mathematical rigor and depth.

item.title: Generalized Noether theorem in the realm of Hamiltonian point dynamics
item.description: arXiv:1206.4449v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Noether's theorem in the realm of point dynamics establishes the correlation of a constant of motion of a Hamilton-Lagrange system with a particular symmetry transformation of its action functional. Although usually derived in the Lagrangian formalism, the Hamiltonian formalism provides a natural context for this correlation. Canonical transformations preserve the canonical form of the action up to a boundary term. Within the class considered here, a symmetry additionally preserves the functional form of the specified extended Hamiltonian. Every smooth phase-space first integral admits locally a corresponding canonical Noether symmetry when momentum-dependent transformations and boundary terms are allowed. In order to represent symmetry mappings that include a transformation of time, we use the extended Hamiltonian formalism. This formalism enables us to define generating functions of canonical transformations that also map time and energy in addition to the conventional mappings of canonical space and momentum variables. The physical energy hypersurface and the choice of the evolution parameter are distinguished from identities on the full extended phase space. As an example, a manifest representation of the symmetry transformation associated with the Runge-Lenz invariant of the Kepler system is derived. A suitable choice of evolution parameter makes its time-shifting representative a symmetry of the specified extended action.
item.dc:creator: J\"urgen Struckmeier
